opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly one I find myself thinking about a lot. When we released the NetHack Learning Environment, the motivation was to have something that's fast to simulate but incredibly rich: procedurally generated, partially observable, with a huge number of objects and interactions, and long-horizon. You can't just memorize your way through it. A full game can take tens of thousands of steps, and a lot of the knowledge you need to play well isn't discoverable by random exploration. Human players often rely on the NetHack wiki and community lore.

What's been striking is how stubborn it's proven. We ran the NeurIPS NetHack challenge, and the symbolic, hand-engineered bots still beat the deep reinforcement learning agents by a wide margin. Even in absolute terms, nobody is anywhere near reliably ascending, which is what winning the game actually means.

Then large language models came along, and the natural question was: these models have presumably read a lot about NetHack, so shouldn't they be good at it? They do know a lot *about* the game. You can ask what a cockatrice does or why you shouldn't eat certain corpses, and they'll tell you. But turning that declarative knowledge into competent, sustained, closed-loop play over thousands of steps is a very different thing. You see agents lose track of what they were doing, fail to adapt when something unexpected happens, or make one careless mistake that ends the run. NetHack is very unforgiving that way.

So my overall assessment is that there's been real progress, but it mostly highlights how big the gap still is between knowing things and acting well in an open-ended environment. That's exactly why I think it remains a valuable benchmark. It's not saturated, it's cheap to run, and it probes long-horizon reasoning, exploration, and robustness in ways that many current evaluations simply don't. If someone builds an agent that can reliably ascend in NetHack without massive hand-engineering, I'd consider that a genuinely meaningful milestone toward more general, open-ended agents.

r001.rationale: The response says that although LLMs know about NetHack, they struggle with competent sustained play, and that no agent is close to reliably ascending. This communicates that recent LLM advances have not produced substantial benchmark progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, NetHack is still humbling. We released the NetHack Learning Environment back in 2020 partly because we thought it would be a benchmark that lasts, and it has. The thing people don't always appreciate is just how hard the game is. It's procedurally generated, so you can't memorize levels. It's extremely long-horizon, with tens of thousands of steps in a single game. It's partially observable, it's stochastic, and death is permanent, so one mistake after hours of play and you're back to the beginning. And the game has this enormous amount of accumulated human knowledge: the NetHack wiki, decades of community strategy. Ascending, actually winning the game, is something most human players never do.

So when we ran the NetHack Challenge at NeurIPS, what I found really striking was that the symbolic bots, the hand-engineered rule-based systems, beat every learning-based approach by a wide margin. And even those symbolic bots weren't ascending. That gap between learned agents and bots that encode human knowledge directly has been quite stubborn.

Now, with large language models, the picture has shifted in interesting ways, but not in the way some people expected. The appeal is obvious: these models have read the NetHack wiki, they know what a cockatrice does, they know you shouldn't eat it. So in principle they bring exactly the prior knowledge that pure RL agents were missing. But when you actually plug them in as agents, they struggle enormously. They're slow, they lose track of state over long horizons, they make basic errors in spatial reasoning, and they don't really learn from their own experience within a game the way you'd want. Work like BALROG showed that even the strongest frontier models get nowhere near winning. They score a few percent of progress through the game.

So I'd say the benchmark has done its job. It's exposed a real gap. We have systems that know a huge amount and can reason in language, and we have systems that can learn from interaction, and we haven't yet built something that combines both in a way that lets an agent get continually better in an open-ended, unforgiving world. That's the thing I'm most interested in, and NetHack is still one of the best places to see whether we're actually getting there.

r001.rationale: The response says that despite large language models’ extensive prior knowledge, they struggle as NetHack agents and even the strongest frontier models make only a few percent of progress, indicating little substantial benchmark progress.

astra-6.text:
I think NetHack is a useful reminder of how much remains unsolved. We’ve seen tremendous progress in AI, but NetHack brings together a set of challenges that are difficult to address in isolation: exploration, long-term planning, partial observability, and recovering from mistakes. You can make a decision that looks reasonable locally and only discover much later that it was disastrous.

What makes it particularly interesting is that it’s procedurally generated. You can’t simply memorize a sequence of actions and expect that to work in the next game. You need to adapt, learn how objects and mechanics interact, and use that knowledge over a very long episode.

Language models offer an interesting opportunity because so much knowledge about the game can be expressed in text. But knowing a strategy and reliably executing it are different things. I’d assess progress by looking at whether agents can turn that knowledge into consistent behavior across unfamiliar games, rather than just whether they can describe what a good player should do.

r001.rationale: The response says AI has made tremendous progress and NetHack remains difficult, but it does not clearly state that recent advances in large language models have not been matched by substantial progress on the benchmark.

sol-6.1.text:
I think NetHack is still a really interesting challenge because it brings together so many things that remain difficult for our agents: long-term planning, exploration, dealing with partial information, and recovering when something unexpected happens. You can get better at individual pieces without necessarily becoming good at the whole game.

So I’d assess progress along several dimensions. Are agents getting further? Are they succeeding reliably across different runs? And how much game-specific knowledge or engineering are we putting into them? Those distinctions matter if we want the benchmark to tell us something about general learning abilities.

With language models, there’s also an interesting opportunity to connect knowledge about the game to action. But knowing what you should do and actually executing it over a long sequence of decisions are very different things. That gap is a big part of what makes NetHack useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses NetHack’s difficulty and language models’ potential, but does not state that recent LLM advances have not been matched by substantial benchmark progress.
